lateo
,

la:verb:lateo.gloss: to conceal, hide, lie hidden, lurk, skulk
senses: to conceal, hide, lie hidden, lurk, skulk
to be hidden and in safety
to live in concealment; to live retired
to be obscure or unknown, lie hidden
la:verb:lateo.html:
lătĕo, ŭi, 2, v. n.
Sanscr. root rah-, forsake; rahas, loneliness, concealment; Gr. ΛΑΘ λανθάνω
,
to lurk, be or lie hid or concealed, to skulk (class.).
Lit.
In gen.: ubi sunt, ubi latent,: cochleae in occulto latent,; cf. : occulte, id.

Agr. 2, 16, 41: clam,: abdite,: in tenebris,: sub nomine pacis bellum latet,: scelus latet inter tot flagitia,: non latuit scintilla ingenii,; : naves latent portu,; cf.: tuta arce,.—Prov.: latet anguis in herba,.—

In partic.
To be hidden, to be in safety: sub umbra amicitiae Romae,; : sub illius umbra Philotas latebam,lurked,.—
Jurid., to lie hid, keep out of sight, in order not to appear before court, .—
Trop.
In gen., to live in concealment, to live retired (rare): crede mihi, bene qui latuit, bene vixit, to lead a retired or quiet life, .—
In partic., analog. to the Gr. λανθάνειν, res latet, to be concealed from, be unknown to one.
with acc. (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; not in Cic.; cf.: fugit me, praeterit me, etc.): latet plerosque, siderum ignes esse, etc.,: nec latuere doli fratrem Junonis,: nil illum latet,: res Eumenem non latuit,; : semen duplex, unum, quod latet nostrum sensum, alterum, quod apertum,.—
With dat.: quae et oculis et auribus latere soleant, Müll.: ubi nobis haec auctoritas tamdiu tanta latuit?: hostique propinquo Roma latet,.—
Absol., to be concealed or obscure, to be unknown: earum causarum aliae sunt perspicuae, aliae latent,: cum laterent hae partes (sc. Galliae),: quae tantum accenderit ignem, Causa latet,: id qua ratione consecutus sit, latet,.—Hence, lătens, entis, P. a., lying hid, hidden, concealed, secret, unknown: saxa latentia,: junctura,: rem latentem explicare definiendo,: animus in aegro corpore,: causas tentare latentes,: Tarquinius mandata latentia nati accipit,. —Comp.: latentior origo,: caussa, id. Civ. Dei, 5, 19.—Absol.: in latenti,in secret, secretly,.—Hence, adv.: lătenter, in secret, secretly, privately: efficere,: amare,: intellegere ex aliqua re,

la:noun:latus.html:
lătus, ĕris, n.
cf. Gr. πλατύς; Lat. lăter, Latium, plautus or plotus
,
the side, flank of men or animals.
Lit.: ego vostra faciam latera lorea,: quid conminatu's mihi? Con. Istud male factum arbitror, quia non latus fodi, : occidisse ex equo dicitur, et latus offendisse vehementer,: cujus latus ille mucro petebat,: laterique accommodat ensem,; ; ; : laterum inclinatione forti ac virili,: vellere latus digitis, to twitch one by the side (in order to attract attention), ; cf.: si tetigit latus acrior,: tum latus ei dicenti condoluisse ... dieque septimo est lateris dolore consumptus,pleurisy,; so, lateris dolor,; ; ; : lateris vigili cum febre dolor,; cf.: laterum dolor aut tussis,: artifices lateris, i. e. those who make skilful side movements or evolutions, ballet-dancers, : latus tegere alicui,to walk by the side of one,: claudere alicui,; and: mares inter se uxoresque contendunt, uter det latus illis (sc. pantomimis),.—Of animals: equorum,: cujus (equi aënei) in lateribus fores essent,.—
Of orators, the lungs: lateribus aut clamore contendere,: quae vox, quae latera, quae vires, etc.,: ut lateris conatus sit ille, non capitis,; cf.: lateris pectorisve firmitas an capitis etiam plus adjuvet,; so : dum vox ac latus praeparetur,; : voce, latere, firmitate (constat orator),: neque enim ex te umquam es nobilitatus, sed ex lateribus et lacertis tuis,: cum legem Voconiam voce magna et bonis lateribus suasissem,: illa adhuc audaciora et majorum, ut Cicero existimat, laterum,.—
Poet., in mal. part., Lucil. ap. ; ; ; : lateri parcere,.—
Transf., in gen.
The side, flank, lateral surface of a thing (opp. frons and tergum; v. h. vv.): collis ex utraque parte lateris dejectus habebat et in frontem leniter fastigatus paulatim ad planiciem redibat,on each side,; cf. : terra angusta verticibus, lateribus latior,: latus unum castrorum,: insula, cujus unum latus est contra Galliam,: et (Fibrenus) divisus aequaliter in duas partis latera haec (insulae) adluit,.—Of a maritime country, the coast, seaboard: Illyricum,: castelli,: tum prora avertit et undis Dat latus,the ship's side,: ubi pulsarunt acres latera ardua fluctus,: nudum remigio,; : dextrum (domus),: mundi,: crystallus sexangulis nascitur lateribus,surfaces,.—Of an army, the flank, : reliquos equites ad latera disponit,: ex itinere nostros latere aperto aggressi,; cf. fin.: ad latus apertum hostium constitui,: ne simul in frontem, simul in latera, pugnaretur,.—So in fighting: latus dare, to expose one's side or flank to the adversary, (v. II. A. infra).—
Esp. freq.: a (ab) latere, on or at the side or flank; a or ab lateribus, on or at the sides or flanks (opp. a fronte, in front, before, and a tergo, at the back, behind): a tergo, a fronte, a lateribus tenebitur,: a fronte atque ab utroque latere cratibus ac pluteis protegebat,; : ab omni latere securus,: ab latere aggredi,: disjectos ab tergo aut lateribus circumveniebant,: ne quis inermibus militibus ab latere impetus fieri posset,: Sulla profligatis iis, quos advorsum ierat, rediens ab latere Mauris incurrit,: si ex hac causa unda prorumperet, a lateribus undae circumfunderentur, : a lateribus, a fronte, quasi tria maria prospectat,.—
Less freq. with ex: latere ex utroque,: ex lateribus aggredi aliquem,: tribus ex lateribus (locus) tegebatur,: ex alio latere cubiculum est politissimum,: omni ex latere armorum molibus urgeri,.—
With de: de latere ire,.—Without prep.: alio latere,.—
Poet. (pars pro toto), the body: penna latus vestit, tenet,: nunc latus in fulvis niveum deponit harenis,; cf. ; 14, 710: forte,: fessum longā militiā,: credidit tauro latus,: liminis aut aquae Caelestis patiens latus,.—
Trop.
In gen.: in latera atque in terga incurrere, to attack the sides, i. e. the unguarded points, : aliena negotia centum Per caput et circa saliunt latus,encompass on every side,: ut a senis latere numquam discederem,never left his side,; cf.: aliquem lateri alicujus adjungere, to attach to his side, i. e. to give him for a companion, ; so, alicui latus dare, of a client, (cf. B. 1. infra): lateri adhaerere gravem dominum,hung about them, threatened them,: Illyriorum rex, lateri ejus haerens, assiduis precibus promissa exigebat,; cf.: Agathocles regis lateri junctus, civitatem regebat,: circumfusa turba lateri meo,.—Esp.: sacpe dabis nudum latus,expose,: la. tus imperii nudum,: nec adulatoribus latus praebeas,expose yourself, lay yourself open to,: latere tecto abscedere, i. e safe, unharmed, : hic fugit omnes Insidias nullique malo latus obdit apertum,: ex uno latere constat contractus,on one side,; so : nulla ex utroque latere nascitur actio,.—
In partic.
To express intimacy, attachment: latus alicui cingere,to cling to,; esp. in the phrase: ab latere, at the side of, i. e. in intimate association with (rare, and perh. not ante-Aug.): ab latere tyranni: addit eos ab latere tyranni,; ; cf.: ille tuum, Castrice, dulce latus,your constant associate,.—
Relationship, kindred, esp. collateral relationship (post-Aug.): quibus (liberis) videor a meo tuoque latere pronum ad honores iter relicturus,: sunt et ex lateribus cognati ut fratres sororesque,: ex latere uxorem ducere,: latus omne divinae domus,: omnes personae cognatorum aut supra numerantur, aut infra, aut ex transverso, sive a latere ... a latere, fratres et sorores, liberique eorum; item parentium fratres et sorores liberique eorum, (Ulp.) de Grad. Cogn. 2 ap. Huschke, Jurisp. Antejust. p. 530.

la:noun:later.html:
lăter, ĕris, m.
Sanscr. root prath-, widen; prathas, breadth; Gr. πλατύς, πλάτος
,
a brick, tile.
Lit.: nil mirum, vetus est maceria, lateres si veteres ruunt, sqq.: in latere aut in caemento, ex quibus urbs effecta est,; cf.: paries crudo latere ac luto constructus,: contabulationem summam lateribus lutoque constraverunt,: lateres de terra ducere,to make,: lateres coquere,to burn,: sepimentum e lateribus coctilibus,burnt bricks,.—Prov.: laterem lavare, to wash a brick, = πλίνθον πλύνειν, i. e. to wash the color out of a brick, to labor in vain, ; but cf. .—
Transf.: lateres aurei, argentei, bars, ingots, or wedges of gold, of silver, ; Varr. ap. ; .

la:noun:latro.html:
lā^tro, ōnis, m.
Gr. λάτρις, root λα-, λαϝ-, in λάω, λεία; cf. lucrum
,
a hired servant, hireling, mercenary, satellite, bodyguard, etc. (only ante-class.): haec effatus ibi, latrones dicta facessunt, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 60 Vahl.).—Of mercenary soldiers: latrones, quos conduxi,: nam hic latro in Sparta fuit,: latronem suam qui auro vitam venditat, Fleck.; cf.: fortunas suas coepere latrones Inter se memorare, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 528 Vahl.); cf. Müll., and the passage from Paul. ex Fest. infra.—
Transf.
A freebooter, highwayman, robber, bandit, irregular soldier, brigand (opp. justi hostes). : latrones eos antiqui dicebant, qui conducti militabant. ἀπὸ τῆς λατρείας. At nunc viarum obsessores dicuntur, Paul. ex Müll.: hostes hi sunt, qui nobis, aut quibus nos publice bellum decrevimus: ceteri latrones aut praedones sunt,: vos latrones et mendicos homines magni penditis?, 75: collecti ex praedonibus latronibusque Syriae,; fin.; : erat ei vivendum latronum ritu, ut tantum haberet, quantum rapere potuisset,: non semper viator a latrone, non numquam etiam latro a viatore occiditur,; cf.: cantabit vacuus coram latrone viator,; : ne quis fur esset, neu latro,: quin etiam leges latronum esse dicuntur, etc.,: quaestio latronum,: qui latronem caedem sibi inferentem, occiderit,.—Of an assassin, .—Poet. of a hunter, .—Of a wolf, .—
For latrunculus, a chessman, a piece in the game of draughts or chess which represents a soldier; a man, pawn (poet.): latronum proelia,: ludere bella latronum,; cf. vitreo latrone,.

la:noun:latrocinium.html:
lā^trōcĭnĭum, ĭi, n.
id.
. *
Military service for pay: apud regem in latrocinio fuisti, Plaut. ap. .—
Transf.
Freebooting, robbery, highway-robbery, piracy (class.): cum illum ex occultis insidiis in apertum latrocinium conjecimus,: fines suos ab latrociniis tueri,: pugna latrocinio magis, quam proelio similis,a contest with robbers,: latrociniis magis quam justo bello gerebantur res,: latrocinium potius quam bellum,: latrociniis ac praedationibus infestatum mare,piracies,; : latrocinia nullam habent infamiam (apud Germanos),: qui in furto aut in latrocinio aut aliqua noxa comprehensi,in robbery,fin.—
In gen., villany, roguery, fraud: furtim et per latrocinia potius, quam bonis artibus, ad imperia et honores nituntur,; cf. .—
Abstr. pro concreto, a band of robbers: si ex tanto latrocinio unus tolletur,.—
Latrocinii imago, the semblance of freebooting, i. e. the game of draughts or chess, which imitates freebooting: sive latrocinii sub imagine calculus ibit,.

la:noun:Latinitas.html:
lătīnĭtas, ātis, f.
Latinus
.
Pure Latin style, Latinity: latinitas est, quae sermonem purum conservat, ab omni vitio remotum. Vitia in sermone, quominus is latinus sit, duo possunt esse: soloecismus et barbarismus, etc.,: secutus sum non dico Caecilium (malus enim auctor latinitatis est), sed Terentium,.—

lātus, a, um, adj.
old Lat. stlātus, Paul. ex ; Sanscr. root star-, strnāmi = sterno; Gr. στορ- in στόρνυμι, στρατός; Lat. sterno, stratus, torus; cf. strāges, struo; not connected with πλατύς, nor with 3. lātus = τλητός
,
broad, wide.
Lit.: fossa,: mare,: via,, § 119: agri,: clavus, (v. clavus): umeri,; cf.: artus barbarorum,: lati et lacertosi viri,broad-shouldered,; : rana bove latior,: palus non latior pedibus quinquaginta,: latissimum flumen,: latissimae solitudines,: comesse panem tris pedes latum,: fossae quindecim pedes latae,: areas latas pedum denum facito,: populi,: moenia lata videt,: latis otia fundis,: ne latos fines parare studeant. : ager,: orbis,: terrae,: lata Polyphemi acies,wide eye,.—Neutr. absol.: crescere in latum,to increase in width, widen,.—Absol.: per latum,: in lato pedum centum,.—
Transf., poet., for proud, swelling (cf. Eng. vulg. spreading): latus ut in circo spatiere,that you may stalk along largely, proudly,: lati incesserunt et cothurnati (histriones),. —
Trop.
In gen., broad, wide, wide-spread, extended (mostly post-Aug.): vox,; cf.: verba,pronounced broadly,: gloria,widespread,: lato Murrus caligat in hoste,: interpretatio,broad, not strict, lenient,: culpa,great,; fin.: fuga,a kind of banishment, whereby all places are forbidden to the exile but one,.—
In partic., of style, diffuse, detailed, copious, prolix: oratio Academicorum liberior et latior (opp. Stoicorum oratio astrictior et contractior),: latum atque fusum,: latiore varioque tractatu,: latiore quadam comprehensione,: genus orandi latum et sonans,: Aeschines his latior et audentior,.— Hence, adv.: lātē, broadly, widely, extensively; with longe, on all sides, far and wide, everywhere.
Lit.: late longeque diffusus,: omnibus longe lateque aedificiis incensis,: minus late vagari,: regnare,: populus late rex,; cf.: diu Lateque victrix,: cladem inferre,.—Comp.: latius demum operaest pretium ivisse,: itaque latius quam caedebatur ruebat (murus),: possidere (agros),: metui,. —Sup.: ager latissime continuatus,: quam latissime possint, ignes faciant,.—
Trop.: ars late patet, widely. : Phrygiae late refer primordia gentis,.—Comp.: latius loquuntur rhetores, dialectici compressius,: quod

pateat latius, of rather extensive application, : latius perscribere,: uti opibus,more lavishly,.—Sup.: fidei bonae nomen latissime manat,: latissime patere,.

la:verb:latro.html:
lātro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.
[cf. Gr. λοιδορέω and λατράζειν = βαρβαρίζειν, Hesych.], to bark (cf. baubor).
Lit.: si canes latrent,; : ne latret canis,: quasi feta canes sine dentibus latrat, Enn. ap. Müll. (Ann. v. 518 Vahl.): canis timidus vehementius latrat quam mordet,: canino rictu,.—Impers. pass.: scit cui latretur cum solus obambulet ipse,.—
Act. for allatrare, to bark at, bay: senem adulterum Latrent Suburanae canes,: cervinam pellem,: nubila,.—Also in pass.: latrari a canibus,.—
Part. pres. as subst.: lātrans, antis, m., a barker, i. e. a dog (poet.): inmeriti fatum latrantis,; plur., .—
Transf.
To resound, roar, of water (poet.): latrantes undae,: (amnis) Alpibus ortus fertur latrantibus undis,; .—
In speaking, to rant, roar, bluster: latrant jam quidam oratores, non loquuntur,: rumperis et latras,.—
Act., to bark at: si quis Obprobriis dignum latraverit,.—
Trop., to bark at, rage, etc.
In gen.: multa ab animalium vocibus tralata in homines, partim quae sunt aperta, partim obscura. Perspicua, ut Ennii: Animus cum pectore latrat, Müll. (cf. Ann. v. 570 Vahl.): admoto latrant praecordia tactu,rage,: curae latrantes,.—
Act.: magnas latrantia pectora curas,.—
In partic.
To demand vehemently: latrare Ennius pro poscere posuit, Paul. ex Müll.; cf. Enn. l. l.: cum sale panis Latrantem stomachum bene leniet,: nil aliud sibi naturam latrare, nisi ut, etc.,.—
Opening the mouth wide, pronounced with a wide mouth: hanc scripsit Latine Plautus cum latranti nomine,.

la:other:Latium.gloss: Latium (a historical region of central Italy, in which the city of Rome was founded and grew to be the capital city of the Roman Empire)
senses: Latium (a historical region of central Italy, in which the city of Rome was founded and grew to be the capital city of the Roman Empire)
la:other:Latium.html:
Lătĭum, ii, n.
2. lătus; Sanscr. root prath-, to spread or widen; cf. Lat. later, etc.; prop., the plains or flat-land; by the ancients referred to latēre, because here Saturnus lay concealed from his son,; ; ; ; or to Latinus,the name of the mythical king, Müll.
,
a country of Italy, in which Rome was situated, now Campagna di Roma, and a part of the Terra di Lavoro, ; Enn. ap. Acro. ad (Ann. v. 455); ; ; ; ; ; ; ; consisting of two parts: Latium vetus,; or antiquum,; ; which was the original territory governed by Rome before the subjugation of the Æqui and Volsci, and: Latium novum, or adjectum,originally the territory of the Æqui, Volsci, Hernici, and Aurunci,.—
Jus Latii, the political rights and privileges which belonged originally to the Latins, but were afterwards granted by the Romans to other people; this jus comprehended less than civitas Romana, but more than peregrinitas (cf. latinitas and Latini): eodem anno Caesar nationes Alpium maritimarum in jus Latii transtulit,. —Also called Latium alone: aut majus est Latium aut minus; majus est Latium, cum et hi, qui decuriones leguntur, et ei qui honorem aliquem aut magistratum gerunt, civitatem Romanam consecuntur; minus Latium est, cum hi tantum, qui vel magistratum vel honorem gerunt, ad civitatem Romanam perveniunt,; cf.: Latium externis dilargiri,: Latio dato,: Latio donata oppida,.—
Hence,
Lătĭ-us, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Latium, Latian, Latin (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): agri,the Latin territory,; ; : gens,; : lingua,: palmes, vines growingin Latium, : boves,. —Poet., for Roman: turba,the Roman people,: parentes,; cf. matres,: annus,the Roman year,: vulnera,of Roman soldiers,.—
Lătīnus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Latium, Latin.
Adj.: populi, the Latins, Enn. ap. Müll. (Ann. v. 24 Vahl.); cf. genus,the Latins, Romans,: lingua,the Latin language, Müll.; cf. opp. Graeca,: poëtae, opp. Graeci,: via, beginning at the Porta Latina, near the Porta Capena, ; ; : dies,the days of the Roman calendar, the Roman year,: feriae, the festival of the allied Latins, which was celebrated especially by offerings to Juppiter Latiaris on Mons Albanus, Müll.; ; ; ; more freq. absol.;v.in the foll. 2.: coloniae, which possessed the jus Latii, ; : nomen, Latin citizenship, also called jus Latii and Latinitas, ; ; (v. socius): casus, i. e. the ablative, Varr. ap. P.: tragici veteres,: esse illud Latinum (verbum),.—Comp.: nihil Latinius legi, M. Aur. ap. Mai.; cf.: nihil Latinius tuis voluminibus,.—Sup.: homo Latinissimus,.—Adv.: Lătīnē, in Latin: Graece haec vocatur emporos: eadem Latine mercator,; : Cumanis petentibus, ut publice Latine loquerentur, et praeconibus Latine vendendi jus esset,in the Latin tongue,: scire,to understand Latin,: num Latine scit?: non enim tam praeclarum est scire Latine, quam turpe nescire,: nescire,: reddere, to translate into Latin, Cic. de Or, 1, 34, 153; cf. docere,.—In partic.: Latine loqui, to speak with propriety or elegance: Latine et diligenter loqui,; cf.: ut pure et emendate loquentes, quod est Latine,: pure et Latine loqui,.—Sometimes, also, like our to talk plain English, for, to speak out, to speak plainly or openly (syn. Romano more loqui): (gladiator), ut appellant ii, qui plane et Latine loquuntur,: Latine me scitote, non accusatorie loqui,: poscere,: formare,to compose in Latin,: componere, id. Gram. init.—Comp.: Latinius, in better Latin (late Lat.), ; .—
Subst.
Lătīni, ōrum, m.
The inhabitants of Latium, Latins, ; sq.; 2, 19 sq.; ; ; ; . —
Those who possessed the Latin rights of citizenship (jus Latii, Latinitas); freq. in the connection, socii et Latini,; ; (v. socius).—
Latini Juniani, freedmen whose liberty was secured by the operation of the lex Junia Norbana (772 A. U. C.), .—
Lătīnae, ārum, f. (sc. feriae), the festival of the allied Latins, the Latin holidays, ; ; ; ; id. poët. Div. 1, 11, 18.—
Lătīnum, i, n., Latin, the Latin language: licet in Latinum illa convertere,: in Latinum vertore,.—
Lătī-nĭensis, e, adj., Latin: populi,: ager, Auct. Harusp. Resp. 10, 20.— In plur absol.: Lătīnĭenses, ĭum, m., the Latins, Auct. Harusp. Resp. 28, 62.—
Lătĭālis, and euphon. collat. form Lă-tĭāris, e (also Lătĭar, v.infra), adj., of or belonging to Latium, Latin.
Form Latialis: populus,the Latins, Romans,: sermo,: Juppiter,; hence, also, caput,a statue of Jupiter,.—Lătĭālĭter, adv., in the Latin manner (post - class.): peplo circa umeros involuto Latialiter tegebatur,: nihil effari,: te Latialiter sonantem, (al. Latiariter).—
Form Latiaris: Latiaris sancte Juppiter (Juppiter Latiaris was the guardian deity of the Latin confederacy, to whom the feriae Latinae were consecrated), : Juppiter, Sillig. N. cr.: collis, Müll.: doctrina Latiaris,.—Adv.: Lătĭārĭter, v.in the preced. 1.—
Hence, subst.: Lătĭar, āris, n., the festival of Jupiter Latiaris: confectum erat Latiar,; cf. .
